en: Taal Volcano produces highly explosive eruptions when rising magma interacts with the water of Taal Lake, generating immense steam pressure.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone bedrock of Palawan, carving out the massive Puerto Princesa Subterranean River cave system over millions of years.
The towering Sierra Madre mountain range blocks moisture-laden southwest monsoon clouds, creating a rain shadow that keeps the Central Luzon plains relatively dry.
Intense tropical rainfall erodes the uplifted marine limestone of Bohol, gradually weathering it into the distinct conical mounds of the Chocolate Hills.
A massive prehistoric volcanic eruption emptied the underlying magma chamber, causing the ground to collapse and form the water-filled Taal Caldera Lake.
Sunlight penetrating the shallow, warm waters of the Sulu Sea allows coral polyps to photosynthesize and rapidly build the massive Tubbataha Reef structure.
The tectonic collision between the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate forces magma upward, continuously shaping Mount Apo's volcanic peak.
The Agusan River slows down as it reaches the coast, causing it to drop carried sediments and continuously expand the Agusan Delta.
Magma beneath Albay heats underground water reservoirs to produce high-pressure steam, which the Tiwi Geothermal Power Plant captures to generate electricity.
The warm Kuroshio Current flows past the eastern coast of Luzon, raising sea temperatures and supporting diverse marine life in the Philippine Sea.
Warm ocean waters in the Philippine Sea evaporate rapidly, providing the latent heat energy that intensifies typhoons before they make landfall.
Geographic isolation on Mindoro restricted the Tamaraw's habitat, causing it to evolve a smaller, dwarf body size compared to mainland water buffalo.
